scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The passamezzo originated in Italy during the 16th century and gained widespread popularity across Europe until roughly 1640.
Early written evidence appears in German lute publications by Hans Neuslider in 1536 and 1540, followed swiftly by extensive adoption in Italy, France, and England.
The form was closely linked to the pavane, with theorists such as Francisco de Salinas noting their interchangeable use in early contexts.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The passamezzo was performed in solo settings, paired social gatherings, or as part of multi-movement musical suites.
It often preceded a faster triple-time dance like the saltarello or gagliarda to balance solemnity with agility.
Today it is a historical tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Dances and Music from the Italian Renaissance / Gastoldi, Gabrieli, Mainerio [...] (https://archive.org/details/youtube-739R9G0qDH8)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The passamezzo is executed in binary rhythm as a flowing, measured court or folk dance.

While choreographies by masters like Fabritio Caroso exist from later decades, original early step descriptions are not preserved, though sources consistently relate its movements to elaborate variants of the pavane.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music for the passamezzo is defined by repeating ostinato bass progressions divided into the minor passamezzo antico and major passamezzo moderno.
It was performed on lutes, keyboards, chitarrones, and chamber ensembles, with notable compositions by Giacomo Gorzanis, Andrea Gabrieli, and Samuel Scheidt.
Listen for the lute, keyboard, chitarrone, chamber ensemble.
The pulse is binary.
A steady, flowing binary rhythm driven by repeating ostinato chord progressions in minor or major, maintaining a calm and measured pace.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures associated with the passamezzo include lutenist Giacomo Gorzanis, who published 24 passamezzi in 1561; theorist Vincenzo Galilei; and composers such as William Byrd, John Bull, Sweelinck, and Bernardo Storace.
Regional variants developed across Europe, including the English 'passingmeasure pavan' for the antico progression and the 'quadro pavan' or 'quadran pavan' for the major-key moderno progression.
The passamezzo evolved in parallel with the pavane and frequently shared structural DNA with related ostinato forms like the romanesca and the follia.

music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Passamezzo (Italy). Meter binary. Instruments: lute, keyboard, chitarrone, chamber ensemble. Form: binary variations over ostinato bass. Mood: tranquil, serious. It should sound like this: A steady, flowing binary rhythm driven by repeating ostinato chord progressions in minor or major, maintaining a calm and measured pace. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.
